comparator.name: Science, Technology & Innovation
comparator.sourceNotes: Full180EC prescribed membership is retained as research, including disputedQuantum6EC; active partial record withholds that unit.54EC specialisation is represented by tenindividualcourses, never added again.

components.name: Engineering the Building Blocks of Life
Design Project
components.note: A compulsory team project follows the selected specialisation. Workshops and preparation run throughout the year, with execution in the final period. Practical participation requires the programme’s safety instruction.

components.name: Quantum Physics 1
components.note: Compulsory in the selected materials track; access for ST&I materials students remains unresolved.

components.name: Advanced Ethical Prototyping
components.note: A full-time eight-week team project develops a physical prototype through design, testing and ethical decisions. It ends with a demonstration, presentation and a partly individual defence. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project; practical work requires safety instruction.

components.name: Bachelor Project Science, Technology & Innovation
components.note: An individual supervised research project includes a thesis and presentation and is examined by at least two UvA examiners. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project. External projects need Examination Board permission.

components.name: Open elective space
components.note: Thirty EC remain open for electives or a minor, normally in the first semester of year three. The study plan is assessed for overlap and approval; at most 12 EC may be introductory subjects, and a foreign minor needs prior approval.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both study wave behaviour and material-related physical principles; the external component extends through light and quantum foundations.
Both investigate energy technologies and evaluate sustainable systems. UCR emphasises technical/economic energy assessment; the external course adds chemical energy-storage and reaction foundations.
Relational databases, SQL and querying overlap with the external client-server/data course; interactive JavaScript/front-end work is not supplied by this UCR course.
Both introduce machine-learning methods and evaluation. The external course specifically applies them to scientific/molecular/material problems; UCR does not guarantee those applications.
Both develop programming and computational problem solving for scientific models; specialised scientific applications differ.
Both develop mathematical foundations for quantitative scientific problems; the external course contextualises these across ST&I themes.
Both develop eigenvalues, matrices and linear-system reasoning. The external course also develops vector calculus and differential equations beyond this UCR course.
Signals, transfer functions, filters and frequency-domain analysis overlap with the electronics component. UCR does not supply the full circuit-building/photonics laboratory.
Both develop statistical data analysis; probability/inference provides a substantive methodological overlap, without asserting identical software or datasets.
Both develop molecular/cellular/biochemical foundations of living systems; disciplinary scope and practical activities differ.

Both use molecular cloning/transformation, PCR and DNA/protein laboratory techniques. The external component additionally covers specific genome-engineering and synthetic-network methods not established here.
Both develop academic inquiry, collaboration, communication and reflection. UCR does not reproduce the full external Makerspace technical-skills component.

Both use iterative design, specifications and project development toward a product. UCR prototypes are developed where feasible, while the external compulsory team project follows a technical specialisation.

comparator.note: A compulsory team project follows the selected specialisation. Workshops and preparation run throughout the year, with execution in the final period. Practical participation requires the programme’s safety instruction.
Compulsory in the selected materials track; access for ST&I materials students remains unresolved.

A full-time eight-week team project develops a physical prototype through design, testing and ethical decisions. It ends with a demonstration, presentation and a partly individual defence. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project; practical work requires safety instruction.

An individual supervised research project includes a thesis and presentation and is examined by at least two UvA examiners. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project. External projects need Examination Board permission.

Thirty EC remain open for electives or a minor, normally in the first semester of year three. The study plan is assessed for overlap and approval; at most 12 EC may be introductory subjects, and a foreign minor needs prior approval.

notes.text: The selected external route includes a 54 EC materials specialisation, sustained physical prototyping and an individual 18 EC research project. UCR research directions provide specific science, computation, circular-resource, life-laboratory and design contributions. Dedicated quantum and condensed-matter depth, instrumentation and the full physical prototype studio remain important limits. No professional engineering equivalence or complete pathway is certified.

audience.programmeDescription: Science, Technology & Innovation at the University of Amsterdam is a Dutch-taught programme combining natural sciences, data and modelling with the design and testing of technological prototypes. This example follows High-tech Designer Materials.
audience.comparisonExplanation: These UCR directions remain provisional while access to compulsory Quantum Physics 1 is confirmed. The active external record shows the supported 174 EC subset.

curriculum.limitation: The confirmed list accounts for 174 credits. Quantum Physics 1 is required in the materials track, but its course-entry rule does not list students from this programme. Access to that six-credit requirement still needs confirmation.

componentNotes.y1-58719: Builds mathematical, statistical and computational foundations and applies them to the programme’s scientific themes.
componentNotes.y1-61760: Studies food systems through nutrient and carbon cycles, agricultural chemistry, farm fieldwork, soil analysis and ethical and social questions.
componentNotes.y1-58696: Introduces computational thinking, algorithms and programming for scientific modelling and simulation.
componentNotes.y1-58958: Develops academic practices, teamwork and design skills, with workshops, a reflective portfolio and practical technical activities.
componentNotes.y1-59419: Introduces cellular building blocks, biochemistry and molecular processes, using microscopy and computational models.
componentNotes.y1-58679: Applies Newtonian mechanics to moving objects and a practical design-and-build task in the Makerspace.
componentNotes.y1-58798: Continues mathematical, statistical and computational skills in the context of second-semester scientific themes.
componentNotes.y1-58951: Develops client-server applications, databases, data cleaning and querying, and interactive web content using JavaScript.
componentNotes.y1-59418: Develops molecular cloning, genome-engineering and bioinformatics techniques through laboratory and computational work.
componentNotes.y1-58768: Continues academic practices, teamwork and technical development through workshops and reflective work.
componentNotes.y1-58799: Studies waves, oscillations, light and their interaction with matter, including the foundations of sensors and optical instruments.
componentNotes.y1-58702: Connects chemical bonding, thermodynamics and reaction kinetics to energy conversion, storage and practical energy technologies.
componentNotes.y2-58706: A compulsory team project follows the selected specialisation. Workshops and preparation run throughout the year, with execution in the final period. Practical participation requires the programme’s safety instruction.
componentNotes.y2-59420: Introduces bonding, crystal structure and electronic behaviour in condensed-matter and materials physics.
componentNotes.y2-58586: Develops vector calculus, eigenvalue methods, complex matrices and systems of differential equations for scientific modelling.
componentNotes.y2-58874: Applies machine learning to scientific problems, including computational representations of molecules and materials.
componentNotes.y2-58521: Combines electronics and photonics with circuit construction, simulation, measurements, filters and spectroscopy.
componentNotes.y2-58760: Develops statistical data analysis and Python programming using a realistic dataset.
componentNotes.y2-59430: Studies fluid and solid mechanics, viscosity, elasticity and viscoelastic behaviour across microscopic and macroscopic scales.
componentNotes.y2-58591: Examines telescopes, microscopes and detectors, linking optical and detector technology to scientific discovery and measurement.
componentNotes.y2-61794: Uses statistical thermodynamics to connect molecular behaviour to material properties, phase transitions and soft-matter systems.
componentNotes.y2-58830: Applies thermodynamics, quantum mechanics and electromagnetism to energy conversion and storage, including semiconductors and batteries.
componentNotes.y3-59335: A full-time eight-week team project develops a physical prototype through design, testing and ethical decisions. It ends with a demonstration, presentation and a partly individual defence. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project; practical work requires safety instruction.
componentNotes.y3-59417: An individual supervised research project includes a thesis and presentation and is examined by at least two UvA examiners. Entry requires the completed first year, at least 120 EC and the Design Project. External projects need Examination Board permission.
componentNotes.y3-open: Thirty EC remain open for electives or a minor, normally in the first semester of year three. The study plan is assessed for overlap and approval; at most 12 EC may be introductory subjects, and a foreign minor needs prior approval.
